faq.question: Can I eat too much protein?
faq.answer: For healthy individuals, excess protein is generally safe. However, extremely high intake (>3 g/kg) may strain kidneys in those with pre-existing kidney conditions. Most people can safely consume up to 2 g/kg daily.

faq.question: Is plant protein as good as animal protein?
faq.answer: Plant proteins can be just as effective when you consume a variety of sources. Combining grains and legumes, like rice and beans, provides all essential amino acids. Some plant proteins like soy are complete on their own.

faq.question: Is BMI accurate for everyone?
faq.answer: No. BMI is a population-level screening tool, not a perfect individual metric. It may overestimate body fat in muscular individuals and underestimate it in elderly people who have lost muscle mass.

faq.question: What BMI is considered obese?
faq.answer: According to WHO standards: BMI 25-29.9 is overweight, 30-34.9 is Class I obesity, 35-39.9 is Class II obesity, and 40+ is Class III obesity. Asian populations may use lower thresholds.

faq.question: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
faq.answer: BMR is your baseline calorie burn at rest. TDEE includes BMR plus calories burned through daily activities and exercise. TDEE is what you use for meal planning.

faq.question: Why did my BMR go down after losing weight?
faq.answer: Weight loss, especially muscle loss, reduces BMR. This is why weight loss plateaus occur. Strength training and adequate protein intake help preserve muscle and maintain BMR during dieting.

faq.question: How often should I recalculate my TDEE?
faq.answer: Recalculate whenever your weight changes by 5+ lbs or 2+ kg, or if your activity level changes significantly. Most people benefit from recalculating every 4-6 weeks during active weight management.

faq.question: Why am I not losing weight despite eating below TDEE?
faq.answer: Common reasons include underestimating portion sizes, not counting liquid calories, metabolic adaptation from prolonged dieting, and inconsistent tracking. Try tracking everything for 2 weeks to identify hidden calories.

faq.question: What is the healthiest body fat percentage?
faq.answer: For men: 10-20% is considered healthy. For women: 20-30% is healthy. Going below essential fat levels can harm hormonal and immune function.

faq.question: Can I target fat loss in specific areas?
faq.answer: No. Spot reduction is a myth. Fat loss occurs throughout the body based on genetics and hormones. Consistent exercise and a calorie deficit reduce overall body fat, including stubborn areas over time.

faq.question: Why is waist-hip ratio better than BMI?
faq.answer: WHR specifically measures abdominal fat, which is more strongly linked to heart disease and diabetes than total body weight. BMI cannot distinguish between harmful belly fat and harmless fat stored elsewhere.

faq.question: How do I measure waist and hip correctly?
faq.answer: Waist: measure at the narrowest point, usually just above the belly button. Hip: measure at the widest point of your buttocks. Use a flexible tape measure, keep it level, and do not pull too tight.

faq.question: How is compound interest different from simple interest?
faq.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on the principal amount. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest. Over time, compound interest grows exponentially while simple interest grows linearly.

faq.question: What is the best compound frequency?
faq.answer: More frequent compounding yields slightly higher returns. However, the difference between monthly and daily compounding is usually small. Focus more on the interest rate than the frequency.

faq.question: Should I choose a 15-year or 30-year mortgage?
faq.answer: 15-year mortgages have lower rates and save tens of thousands in interest, but higher monthly payments. Choose 15-year if you can comfortably afford the payments. Otherwise, take 30-year and make extra principal payments when possible.

faq.question: How much should my down payment be?
faq.answer: Ideally 20% to avoid Private Mortgage Insurance. However, many programs allow 3-10% down. Consider your emergency fund, closing costs, and maintenance reserves when deciding your down payment amount.

faq.answer: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing the principal. APR includes the interest rate plus fees and closing costs. APR gives you a more accurate comparison between different loan offers.

faq.question: Should I choose a longer or shorter loan term?
faq.answer: Shorter terms have higher monthly payments but lower total interest. Choose the shortest term you can comfortably afford. If cash flow is tight, a longer term provides flexibility, and you can always make extra payments.

faq.question: Is the 4% rule still valid today?
faq.answer: Many experts now recommend 3.3-3.5% for 30-year retirements due to lower expected future returns and longer lifespans. The original 4% rule was based on historical US data that may not repeat.

faq.question: Does the 4% rule account for inflation?
faq.answer: Yes. You increase your withdrawal each year by inflation. So if you withdraw $40,000 in year 1 and inflation is 3%, you withdraw $41,200 in year 2. The initial 4% is calculated once at retirement.

faq.question: How much do I need to retire comfortably?
faq.answer: A common rule is 25x your annual expenses. If you need $50,000/year, aim for $1.25 million. However, this varies by lifestyle, location, healthcare needs, and desired retirement age.

faq.question: What if I started saving late?
faq.answer: It is never too late. Increase your savings rate to 20-30%, delay retirement by a few years, downsize your lifestyle, or consider part-time work in early retirement.

faq.answer: It works for anything that compounds: savings accounts, bonds, stocks, GDP growth, and inflation. It is an approximation, but accurate enough for quick mental math across most realistic return ranges.

faq.question: Why 72 and not a round number?
faq.answer: 72 is divisible by many numbers, making mental math easy. For very low rates, 70 is slightly more accurate. For high rates, 69.3 is mathematically precise.

faq.question: What is a good ROI?
faq.answer: It depends on the investment type and risk level. Stocks historically return 7-10% annually. Real estate often yields 8-12%. A good ROI should exceed the risk-free rate plus a suitable risk premium.

faq.question: Does ROI include all costs?
faq.answer: It should, but often does not. Include purchase price, transaction fees, maintenance costs, taxes, and opportunity cost. Forgetting hidden costs is the most common mistake when calculating ROI.

faq.question: Is 5% ROI good?

faq.question: Can I get 20% ROI consistently?

faq.question: Which is better for comparing savings accounts?
faq.answer: Always use APY for savings. Two accounts can have the same APR but different APYs if they compound at different frequencies. APY reflects the actual amount you will earn in a year.

faq.question: Why do credit cards show APR instead of APY?
faq.answer: Credit cards use APR because regulations require it, and it makes the rate appear lower than the actual cost. Credit card interest compounds daily, so the effective APY is typically 1-2% higher than the stated APR.
